In 2003, Wellesley limited class average grades in lower-level courses to no higher than a B+. In 2004, Princeton limited As in each department to 35% for undergraduate course work.

Both policies were unpopular with students & were discontinued.

In 2003, Wellesley limited class average grades in lower-level courses to no higher than a B+. In 2004, Princeton limited As in each department to 35% for undergraduate course work.

Both policies were unpopular with students & were discontinued.

The second wave of grade inflation occurred during the 1980s, when the student-participation movement became more prevalent & had more serious stakes.

In 1973, 29% of colleges used student evaluations—by 1993, it rose to 94%. The evaluations became tied to tenure & promotions.

During the 1970s, university administrators worried about an enrollment crisis spurred by high inflation and about the end of the college-age baby boom cohort. 

They needed to find ways to attract students—one way to do so was by grading more leniently.

At Harvard, A-range grades made up 85% of all letter grades in 2024-25. At Yale, ~79% of students received A-range grades in 2022-23. More than 70% of students at Emory College had a GPA of 3.5 or higher in 2025.

Grade inflation has been an issue since at least the 1960s. 🧵
